Release of non-methane organic compounds during simulated landﬁlling
of aerobically pretreated municipal solid waste
Yuanyuan Zhang a, Dongbei Yue a,*, Jianguo Liu a, Peng Lu b, Ying Wang c, Jing Liu b, Yongfeng Nie a
a Key Laboratory for Solid Waste Management and Environment Safety, Ministry of Education of China, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China

a b s t r a c t
Characteristics of non-methane organic compounds (NMOCs) emissions during the anaerobic decom-
position of untreated (APD-0) and four aerobically pretreated (APD-20, APD-39, APD-49, and APD-63)
samples of municipal solid waste (MSW) were investigated in laboratory. The cumulative mass of the
NMOCs of APD-20, APD-39, APD-49, and APD-63 accounted for 15%, 9%, 16%, and 15% of that of APD-0,
respectively. The intensities of the NMOC emissions calculated by dividing the cumulative NMOC
emissions by the quantities of organic matter removed (QVS) decreased from 4.1 mg/kg QVS for APD-0 to
0.8e3.4 mg/kg QVS for aerobically pretreated MSW. The lipid and starch contents might have signiﬁcant
impact on the intensity of the NMOC emissions. Alkanes dominated the NMOCs released from the
aerobically pretreated MSW, while oxygenated compounds were the chief component of the NMOCs
generated from untreated MSW. Aerobic pretreatment of MSW prior to landﬁlling reduces the organic
content of the waste and the intensity of the NMOC emissions, and increases the odor threshold, thereby
reducing the environmental impact of landﬁlls.

1. Introduction
More than 80% of municipal solid waste (MSW) generated in
China with characteristics of high moisture and food waste content
was disposed of in landﬁlls in 2008. The degradation of MSW may
lead to a long-term threat to the environment and public health,
such as the risk of groundwater pollution due to leachate seepage,
fugitive greenhouse gas emissions contributing to climate change,
and odor pollution caused by non-methane organic compounds
(NMOCs), which is direct harassment to adjacent urban commu-
nities. Although NMOCs comprise less than 1% (v/v) of typical
landﬁll gas, they may create a disproportionate environmental
burden and potential risk to human health (Allen et al., 1997). For
example, emissions of carcinogens, such as benzene and vinyl
chloride, pose a potential threat to workers and local inhabitants
(El-Fadel et al.,1997; Durmusoglu et al., 2010). Furthermore, chloro-
and ﬂuoro-hydrocarbons emitted from landﬁlls seriously corrode
combustion engines that utilize landﬁll gas (Dernbach, 1985),
deplete the ozone layer, and cause climate change (Molina and
Rowland, 1974; Wallington et al., 1994). NMOCs are imposing
such a signiﬁcant impact on the environment that the investigation
of their generation and mitigation has been receiving increasing
attention (Eklund et al., 1998; Zou et al., 2003; de la Rosa et al.,
2006; Chiriac et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008; Saral et al., 2009;
Raco et al., 2010).
Methods that can mitigate release of the NMOCs to the atmo-
sphere include (1) installation of a gas recovery, collection, and
treatment system, such as an activated-carbon ﬁxed bed for NMOCs
adsorption (Shin et al., 2002; Pagans et al., 2006); and (2)
emplacement of cover soil with microbial activities, which has been
shown to be efﬁcient at oxidizing NMOCs. For example, some
methanotrophs have been found to be able to metabolize rapidly
a variety of aliphatic compounds, halogenated halocarbons, and
aromatics (Scheutz et al., 2008; Tassi et al., 2009). In addition,
Scheutz and Kjeldsen (2005) found that halogenated organic
compounds were dechlorinated under anoxic conditions, and the
generated degradation products were removed under aerobic
conditions. More recently, He et al. (2010) investigated the effect of
oxygen content on the release of NMOCs during the initial
decomposition of MSW and indicated that high-level ventilation
reduced NMOC emissions. Since aerobic degradation processes
considerably decrease NMOC emissions, aerobic pretreatment of
MSW may also produce desired effect on reduction of NMOCs
during landﬁlling.

Aerobic pretreatment of MSW is commonly believed to be an
effective method to reduce the mass of waste and improve landﬁll
behavior. Compared to the original MSW, pollutant concentrations
generated from aerobically pretreated MSW within a landﬁll can
remarkably decrease in terms of chemical oxygen demand(COD) and
nitrogen in the leachate (Leikam and Stegmann,1999; Tränkler et al.,
2002; Kuruparan et al., 2003; Bayard et al., 2008; Gunawardana et al.,
2009). Besides, the biogas production potential can also be produced
(Zach et al., 2000; Bockreis and Steinberg, 2005; Lornage et al., 2007).
To our knowledge, however, neither has the impact of aerobic
pretreatment on characteristics of NMOCs generated during anaer-
obic stage nor the release of NMOCs from the anaerobic degradation
of aerobically pretreated MSW been reported.
The objective of this research was to characterize the NMOC
emissions of aerobically pretreated MSW samples during anaerobic
decomposition by measuring the NMOC yields and components
and the extent of MSW degradation, and by analyzing emission
intensities. The effectiveness of aerobic pretreatment of MSW in
reducing NMOCs was also discussed.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. MSW sample
About 500 kg MSW sample was obtained from the Beishenshu
landﬁll in Beijing, China. The sample was manually tumbled and
mixed before the experiments. The composition of the sample
obtained by manual sorting is presented in Table 1. The moisture
(wet basis), volatile solid (VS), and total carbon contents of the
sample were 64.5%, 65.1%, and 34.9%, respectively.
2.2. Column experiments
To estimate the amount of released NMOCs during anaerobic
degradation of MSW following different aerobic pretreatments,
a set of column experiments consisting of ﬁve reactors (R0eR4) was
performed for 127 d. The reactors were made of high-density
polyethylene. Each had an internal diameter of 500 mm and
a height of 750 mm (Fig. 1).
Each reactor was ﬁlled with 77.5 kg (wet weight) of raw MSW
sample at a height of 60 cm. All reactors, except for R0 which was
operated anaerobically throughout the study, were initially oper-
ated aerobically at various aeration rates for 30e50 d. The
normalized indicator “aerobic pretreatment degree” (APD) was
calculated by dividing the amount of organic solid degraded during
aerobic stage by the original amount. Accordingly, the wastes that
were to be treated anaerobically were labeled as APD-0, APD-20,
APD-39, APD-49 and APD-63, respectively. The operation modes
are shown in Table 2. Aerobically pretreated wastes were the initial
wastes for the anaerobic degradation. Subsequently, the reactors
R1eR4 were operated under anaerobic conditions with efﬁcient
sealing. The accumulated NMOCs in the reactors during the
anaerobic stage were analyzed on the 127th day.
2.3. Analytical methods
Moisture content was determined by heating the ground sample
at 105 C for 24 h and expressed on a wet basis. The VS content was
determined by ashing the dry samples at 550 C to the constant
weight in a mufﬂe furnace (Zhang et al., 2008). Crude protein was
determined by multiplying Kjeldahl nitrogen (KN) content by the
factor 6.25 (APHA, 1998). Lipid was extracted with petroleum ether
for 6 h and then quantiﬁed by measuring the mass loss of the
residue after combustion (AOAC, 1990, method 920.39). Crude ﬁber
was analyzed according to AOAC (1990) method 962.09. The
amount of starch was determined by subtracting the sum of lipid,
protein, and ﬁber contents from the biologically degradable matter
(BDM). The analytical procedure and calculation for BDM were the
same as those described for COD (Wang et al., 2003), except that the
analysis was performed at room temperature.
A 6 L SUMMA canister was used to collect the gas sample. The
sample was concentrated into a cold trap which contains two beds
of sorbent, i.e. Tenax TA and Carbograph, supported by quartz wool
before analysis by gas chromatography coupled with ﬂame ioni-
zation detector. The measurement setup consisted of a ﬂow
controller, a thermal desorber (Markes International, UK), and a gas
chromatograph (GC6890, Agilent, USA) equipped with a ﬂame
ionization detector and jet-modulated parts (KT2001, Zeox, USA)
for
comprehensive
two-dimensional
gas
chromatography
(GC  GC) according to the method used by Xu et al. (2003). The
sampling and desorption control software (Markes International,
UK) and ChemStation (Agilent, USA) installed on a personal
computer were used to control the sampling/thermal desorption
system and the gas chromatograph, respectively.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characteristics of aerobically pretreated waste
Aerobic pretreatment produced obvious impact on the compo-
sition of the treated waste (Table 3). Higher aeration strength led to
lower VS content. Moreover, easily degradable components, such as
lipids, starch, and proteins, contributed to the loss of organic
matter. The lipids were almost entirely removed during aerobic
pretreatment. The amounts of starch were reduced by 30.4%, 40.7%,
77.7%, and 89.7% in R1 (APD-20), R2 (APD-39), R3 (APD-49), and R4
(APD-63), respectively. Protein and ﬁber were degraded slowly; the
maximum amounts of reduction were only 28.2% and 37.0%,
respectively.
The modes of aeration inﬂuenced the degradation rate of
organic matter in the waste. Based on the organic losses during
aerobic pretreatment of the MSW, aeration at 10 L min1 m3 in R1
was not adequate, and the growth of aerobic microorganisms was
limited, which resulted in slow decomposition. In contrast, aeration
at 60 L min1 m3 could supply sufﬁcient oxygen for the degra-
dation of organic matter, based on the decrease in the amount of
starch.

3.2. Yields of NMOCs
NMOCs can be classiﬁed into ﬁve categories: oxygenated
compounds (ketones, alcohols, aldehydes, acids, and esters),
alkanes, alkenes, aromatics, and chlorinated compounds (Ran et al.,
2009). They originate from intermediates or ﬁnal products of
organic matter decomposition and from organic chemicals present
in MSW (e.g., household cleaning products). The majority of
oxygenated compounds, alkanes, and alkenes are decomposition
by-products of easily degradable organic matter (Smet et al., 1999);
while most chlorinated compounds result from direct volatilization
of solid waste components in the landﬁll, and their levels depend
on vapor pressure relationships under landﬁll conditions (SEPA,
2004). Chlorinated compounds are produced in the largest quan-
tities by the chemical industry for use in consumer products
(Environmental Agency, 2002). Aromatics also may be present in
MSW. Most aromatics are lipophilic compounds that can be
absorbed by lipids (He et al., 2010). In addition, aromatics are
possible by-products of lignin degradation, since lignin has an
aromatic structure.
The cumulative NMOC yields during the anaerobic processes for
each waste are presented in Table 4. The NMOC quantities released
by APD-0 were higher than those released by aerobically pretreated
waste. The cumulative weights of the NMOCs generated from APD-
20, APD-39, APD-49, and APD-63 accounted for 15%, 9%, 16%, and
15% of that of APD-0, respectively. The APD-0 sample contained
high starch, lipid, and protein contents. Until the 127th day, the
leachate pH was stable below 5.6; this means that APD-0 was still in
the hydrolysis acidiﬁcation stage. Considerable acidiﬁcation of
organic matter inhibits the conversion of organic intermediates to
CO2 and CH4. Hence, NMOCs, especially of biogenic origins, cannot
be further degraded. Aerobic pretreatment of MSW noticeably
reduced the emission of NMOCs during the anaerobic period.
Besides a decrease in organic content of pretreated wastes, this
phenomenon may also be attributed to the reduction in NMOCs’
emissions levels of pretreated organic matter. To investigate this
possibility, the emission intensity of NMOCs were calculated by
dividing the cumulative NMOC emissions by the quantities of
organic matter removed during the anaerobic period (QVS), which
are also shown in Table 4.
The emission intensity of NMOCs decreased from 4.1 mg/kg QVS
for APD-0 to 0.8e3.4 mg/kg QVS for aerobically pretreated waste.
This indicates that fewer NMOCs were generated from aerobically
pretreated waste than from raw waste, based on a unit weight of
anaerobically degraded organic matter. Aerobic pretreatment
effectively reduced the NMOC emission levels and the organic
content of the waste. The reduction effectiveness, however,
decreased from 82% to 20% (compared with APD-0) with the
enhancement of aerobic pretreatment from APD-20 to APD-63. The
compositions of the aerobically pretreated waste probably caused
the differences in the NMOC emission levels. The protein and ﬁber
contents did not vary much from APD-0 to APD-63. Compared with
APD-0, APD-20 and APD-39 (from which the smallest NMOC
emission levels were measured) contained relatively low lipid and
starch contents, which accounted for 7.7% and 69.6% for APD-20,
and 3.8% and 59.3% for APD-39, respectively. The amount of
starch was further reduced to 22.2% and 10.3% with the enhance-
ment of aerobic treatment in APD-49 and APD-63, respectively.
Lipid and starch contents may have a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on the
intensity of NMOC emissions. Additional research is necessary to
investigate this hypothesis.

investigated according to the total NMOC concentrations of each
category shown in Table 5. For APD-0, oxygenated compounds

composed 66.0% of the total mass of NMOCs. For APD-20 to APD-63,
alkanes were the dominant NMOCs, which accounted for approx-
imately 48.5%, 56.5%, 66.4%, and 56.8%, respectively. The percentage
of ketones decreased signiﬁcantly from APD-0 to APD-63, whereas
that of chlorinated and aromatic compounds increased somewhat.
Oxygenated compounds, including ketones, alcohols, aldehydes,
and esters, are normally observed during the initial decomposition
of food waste, which coincide with the conditions of APD-0. The
main oxygenated compounds for APD-0 were ketones; this obser-
vation agrees with the results of He et al. (2010).
Nagata (2003) investigated the odor threshold distribution for
NMOCs. Thresholds are distributed in a wide concentration range,-
depending on the odor substances. The top of the threshold
distribution is 10e100 ppb for oxygenated compounds, 100 ppb
to 1 ppm for hydrocarbons, and 1e10 ppm for chlorinated
compounds.

oxygenated
compounds < hydrocarbons < chlorinated compounds. Humans are
normally more sensitive to NMOCs with lower odor thresholds. They
are more sensitive to the odor from untreated waste than that from
aerobically pretreated waste with the same NMOC concentration.

4. Conclusions
The yields and compositions of NMOCs from landﬁlling of
aerobically pretreated MSW under laboratory conditions were
investigated. The cumulative mass of NMOCs of aerobically pre-
treated MSW (APD-20, APD-39, APD-49 and APD-63) accounted for
15%, 9%, 16%, and 15% of that of raw MSW (APD-0), respectively. The
NMOC emission levels decreased from 4.1 mg/kg QVS for APD-0 to
0.8e3.4 mg/kg QVS for aerobically pretreated MSW, and they
increased as the aeration rate increased during aerobic pretreat-
ment. Lipid and starch contents may inﬂuence the NMOC emission
levels. The main categories of NMOCs for raw and aerobically pre-
treated MSW were oxygenated compounds and alkanes, respec-
tively. It was found that pretreated MSW produced less intense
odors. Aerobic pretreatment of MSW prior to landﬁlling reduces the
organic content of waste, decreases the intensity of NMOC emis-
sion, and increases the odor threshold, thereby reducing the
negative environmental impacts of landﬁlls.
